title: Load Balancing Fundamentals
summary: What a load balancer does, where it sits in the request path, and the L4-vs-L7 distinction that decides what it can see and act on.

slides.markdown:
A **load balancer** sits between clients and a fleet of backend servers, spreading requests across them so no single machine takes the whole load — and so the fleet keeps serving even when one node dies. Any service with more than one instance needs one.

Think of it as a maitre d' directing customers to open tables: send everyone to the same table and it drowns while the rest sit empty. This topic covers what a load balancer actually does, the L4-vs-L7 split, and the redundancy trap of running just one.

slides.sectionTitle: What a load balancer actually does
slides.markdown:
A load balancer sits between clients and a pool of backend servers and decides, request by request, which server handles it. Without one, every client would need to know every server's address, and one overloaded or dead server would take down whichever clients happened to be pointed at it.

Concretely: three app servers each comfortably handle ~1,000 req/s. Point all traffic at one directly and the whole system caps at 1,000 req/s; put a load balancer in front and the same three servers serve ~3,000 req/s combined, and losing one still leaves ~2,000 req/s of capacity.

The load balancer is also the first place failure gets handled — it can stop sending traffic to a server the moment that server looks unhealthy.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: where the load balancer sits — client, LB, app tier
slides.markdown:
![Client requests routed through load balancer to app servers](assets/request-path.svg)

The load balancer sits directly in the request path, not off to the side: every request from the client hits the load balancer first, and only then reaches whichever app server it picks. The client never talks to an app server directly — it only ever knows the load balancer's address, often a single DNS name or a virtual IP shared by a small cluster of load balancers for their own redundancy.

That single entry point is what lets you add, remove, or replace app servers without the client ever noticing — the load balancer is the only thing that has to know the current server list.

slides.sectionTitle: L4 vs L7 load balancing: what each layer can see and do
slides.markdown:
A **Layer 4** load balancer routes based on IP address and TCP/UDP port alone — it never looks inside the packet's payload. A **Layer 7** load balancer terminates the connection and reads the actual HTTP request — path, headers, host, cookies, even the body — before deciding where it goes.

| | L4 | L7 |
|---|---|---|
| Sees | IP + port | Full HTTP request (path, headers, host) |
| Routes on | Which port opened the connection | URL path, header value, cookie |
| Overhead | Lower — just forwards packets | Higher — terminates TLS, parses HTTP |
| Examples | AWS NLB, raw TCP/LVS | AWS ALB, NGINX, Envoy, HAProxy (HTTP mode) |

**How to decide:** if you need to route `/api/*` to one fleet and `/static/*` to another, or read a cookie for sticky sessions, you need L7 — an L4 balancer physically cannot see that far into the request.

slides.sectionTitle: Hardware vs software vs cloud-managed load balancers
slides.markdown:
Load balancers come in three flavors that trade cost, control, and operational burden. **Hardware appliances** (F5 BIG-IP is the classic example) are dedicated boxes — extremely fast, expensive, and you own patching and capacity planning. **Software load balancers** (NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy) run as ordinary processes on commodity servers or containers — cheaper and flexible, but you still operate them yourself.

**Cloud-managed load balancers** (AWS ALB/NLB, Google Cloud Load Balancing) are a managed service: you configure rules and the provider handles scaling, patching, and multi-zone availability.

Most new systems default to cloud-managed for the app tier and reach for software LBs like Envoy when they need control cloud offerings don't expose — custom routing logic, service-mesh integration, or on-prem deployment.

slides.sectionTitle: A single load balancer as a new single point of failure — and the fix
slides.markdown:
Putting one load balancer in front of many servers fixes the app tier's single-point-of-failure problem — and quietly creates a new one at the load balancer itself. If that one box or process dies, every server behind it becomes unreachable even though all of them are healthy.

The fix is to make the load balancer tier redundant too: run at least two instances behind a mechanism that survives one dying — a floating virtual IP managed by keepalived/VRRP, DNS with health-checked failover, or simply a cloud provider's managed LB, which is already redundant across availability zones internally.

The pattern repeats at every layer of a system: whatever sits in front of a redundant tier must itself be made redundant, or you've moved the single point of failure, not removed it.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: putting one load balancer in front without redundancy
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I added a load balancer, so my app tier is now highly available."

**Why it's wrong:** a lone load balancer instance is itself a single point of failure. You've made the app tier redundant while leaving an even more critical single box in front of it — if it fails, every healthy app server behind it becomes unreachable at once, which is worse than losing one app server ever was.

**Correct model:** redundancy has to apply to every tier in the request path, including the load balancer itself. Run at least two LB instances with automatic failover — VRRP/keepalived, or a cloud provider's zone-redundant managed LB — never a single instance in production.
